title: Remote Infrared Absorption Spectroscopy with Undetected Photons
authors: Simon Neves, Fériel Armbruster, Jean-Pierre Wolf
abstract: We demonstrate a novel method for remote open-path Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy with undetected photons. Similar to previous quantum spectroscopy works, a mid-infrared spectrum is reconstructed by detecting a near-infrared radiation only, thus bypassing important limitations of infrared detectors. Our study however relies on the co-propagation of the photon-pair and the pump-laser over the same optical path, which allows the probing of the open atmosphere over long distances. By sending the photons over unprecedented distances of up-to 43.4m in the outdoor atmosphere, we were able to detect butane released in the open-path, as well as natural atmospheric methane, thus demonstrating the first use of infrared spectroscopy with undetected photons for atmospheric measurements.
summary: The paper presents a breakthrough technique for remote infrared gas sensing using quantum light sources (biphotons) in an open-path geometry. By detecting only near-infrared photons while probing mid-infrared absorption features, the method bypasses limitations of traditional IR detectors. This allows for long-distance, field-deployable measurements of atmospheric gases like methane and butane.
main_problem: To develop a novel, remote method for Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy capable of measuring gas concentrations in the open atmosphere by utilizing quantum light sources.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated this technique over distances up to 43.4 m, achieving the first measurement of atmospheric methane and butane using undetected photons.
method: The method relies on a nonlinear interferometric setup driven by Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion (SPDC) to generate correlated photon pairs, allowing the mid-infrared spectrum to be reconstructed solely by detecting near-infrared signal photons.
model_or_system: The system uses a quantum nonlinear interferometer interrogated by a triple beam (pump, signal, idler) sent over an open path. The core principle involves measuring the signal photon flux as a function of tunable idler retardance to reconstruct the absorption spectrum via Fourier transform.
key_observables:
Signal photon flux $P_s(x)$, reconstructed spectral intensity $I(
u)$, and calculated absorbance $A(
u)$ for specific gases like $	ext{CH}_4$ and n-butane.
important_parameters: Open path length ($L$) up to 43.4 m; low gain regime ($n \ll 1$); spectral resolution limited by the window function (e.g., $0.53 	ext{ cm}^{-1}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a monochromatic pump laser and that the ambient air is relatively non-dispersive for initial simplifications; saturation of water vapor remains a major limitation.
figures_summary: Figures show stable nonlinear interferometers over long paths, measured signal-photon interferograms corresponding to reconstructed spectra (e.g., methane/water vapor), and comparisons of calculated absorbance against HITRAN data.
paper_structure: The paper details the quantum physical setup using SPDC in PPLN, describes the measurement process involving an open-path nonlinear interferometer, derives the relationship between signal flux and spectral absorbance, and validates the technique by measuring known gases ($	ext{CH}_4$, n-butane) over long outdoor paths.
why_interesting: This work represents a significant application of quantum optics to fundamental sensing problems. The ability to perform remote spectroscopy without complex mid-IR detectors is highly relevant for developing field-deployable quantum sensors, bridging quantum physics with atmospheric science and metrology.
